Clinical Neurology & Neuro-Anatomy Curriculum 150 Master Cases

Clinical Neuro-Localisation Challenges

Curated by Anupam Singh, MD, Professor, Department of Medicine, Santosh Medical College. A rigorous, progressive 10-tier clinical curriculum designed to transition learners from first-principles anatomical reasoning to expert discriminative mastery. Organized in the progressive sequence recommended by teaching_style.txt: moving from gross central-vs-peripheral triage, through longitudinal tract systems, vertical cord levels, cranial nerves, brainstem crossed principles, cerebellar-vs-sensory ataxia, cortical lobes, deep subcortex, to advanced grand-round discriminators.

📖 Instructions to Students: The 5-Question Diagnostic Method

"Neurological localisation is pattern recognition based on anatomy. Do not diagnose 'stroke', 'tumour' or 'multiple sclerosis' first. First state the anatomical locus and pathways involved; only then ask what caused it."

Core Foundations of Clinical Neuro-Localisation

Anatomical rules, brainstem geography, aphasia flows, and tract matrices to anchor systematic diagnosis.
Core Axiom (teaching_style.txt): "Don't memorise 100 syndromes. Learn about 15 anatomical rules. Then every case becomes a combination of those rules."
➜
Cortical signs (aphasia, neglect, seizure, agnosia) → Cerebral Cortex
➜
Same-side face + body sensory loss → Above Brainstem / Thalamocortical
➜
Crossed face (one side) + body (opposite) → Brainstem lesion
➜
Cranial nerve palsy + opposite hemiparesis → Brainstem crossed syndrome
➜
Sensory level across trunk → Spinal Cord
➜
LMN signs at level + UMN signs below → Segmental Spinal Cord
➜
Symmetric saddle anesthesia + early bladder → Conus Medullaris
➜
Asymmetric painful flaccid leg weakness → Cauda Equina (Roots)
➜
Dermatomal sensory + myotomal motor → Spinal Nerve Root
➜
Isolated named peripheral nerve territory → Peripheral Nerve
➜
Same-side limb dysmetria & ataxia → Cerebellar Hemisphere
➜
Impaired proprioception + positive Romberg → Dorsal Column / Large Fiber Pathway
➜
Dense pure motor/sensory without cortical signs → Deep Hemisphere / Internal Capsule / Thalamus

1. What functions are abnormal?

Map all affected systems: motor power, sensation, cranial nerves, visual fields, speech/language, coordination, and autonomic control.

2. Central or Peripheral?

UMN signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity, Babinski) → Brain/Spinal cord. LMN signs (wasting, fasciculations, areflexia) → Anterior horn/root/plexus/nerve.

3. Is there a "Level"?

Cortical signs → Cortex; Crossed signs → Brainstem; Sharp sensory level → Spinal cord; Dermatome → Root; Single nerve → Peripheral nerve.

4. Which side is the lesion on?

Cerebral cortex/subcortex → Contralateral body; Cerebellum → Ipsilateral limbs; Brainstem → Ipsilateral cranial nerve + contralateral body.

5. Which neighbouring structures must lie together?

The essence of localisation: Find the unique anatomical nexus where the affected cranial nerve fascicles, motor tracts, and sensory pathways converge in a single compact volume.

The Rule of 4s (Peter Gates): A 4-part mental framework to master brainstem stroke syndromes in seconds.

Clinical Sign Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) Lesion Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) Lesion
Weakness Distribution Pyramidal pattern (Extensors > Flexors in arms; Flexors > Extensors in legs) Focal segmental (isolated nerve, root, or anterior horn cell distribution)
Muscle Tone Spasticity (velocity-dependent clasp-knife rigidity) Flaccidity / Hypotonia
Deep Tendon Reflexes Hyperreflexia, clonus, spread of reflex zones Hyporeflexia or complete areflexia
Plantar Response Extensor (Babinski sign positive), Oppenheim/Chaddock signs Flexor or absent
Muscle Bulk Disuse atrophy only (slow, mild) Neurogenic wasting / Denervation atrophy (early, severe)
Fasciculations Absent Frequently present (spontaneous motor unit twitches)

The 3-Question Aphasia Decision Flowchart: Assess (1) Fluency → (2) Comprehension → (3) Repetition.

Aphasia Type Spontaneous Fluency Auditory Comprehension Repetition Classic Anatomical Localization
Broca Aphasia Nonfluent (effortful, telegraphic) Preserved Impaired Left inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis/opercularis, Brodmann 44/45)
Transcortical Motor Nonfluent Preserved Preserved Left dorsolateral prefrontal / SMA watershed anterior to Broca
Wernicke Aphasia Fluent (paraphasic, jargon) Impaired Impaired Left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann 22)
Transcortical Sensory Fluent Impaired Preserved Left temporo-parieto-occipital junction (sparing Wernicke area)
Conduction Aphasia Fluent Preserved Markedly Impaired Left arcuate fasciculus / supramarginal gyrus (Brodmann 40)
Global Aphasia Nonfluent Impaired Impaired Entire left perisylvian region (combined MCA superior + inferior divisions)
Mixed Transcortical Nonfluent Impaired Preserved Isolation of perisylvian language arc (bilateral watershed infarcts)
Anomic Aphasia Fluent Preserved Preserved Dominant angular gyrus or left anterior/inferior temporal lobe

Brown-Séquard (Hemicord)

  • Ipsilateral below lesion: UMN spastic weakness (corticospinal) + loss of vibration & joint-position sense (dorsal column).
  • Contralateral below lesion: Loss of pain & temperature (spinothalamic) starting 1–2 segments below level.
  • At lesion level: Ipsilateral LMN signs & complete sensory band.

Anterior Spinal Artery

  • Bilateral below lesion: Paraplegia / quadriplegia (corticospinal) + loss of pain & temperature (spinothalamic).
  • Spared: Dorsal columns intact (vibration, 2-point discrimination & proprioception preserved).
  • Sphincters: Acute urinary retention & autonomic paralysis.

Central Cord / Syringomyelia

  • Dissociated sensory loss: "Cape-like" loss of pain & temperature over shoulders/arms with light touch spared (anterior commissure decussation disrupted).
  • Arms > Legs: Hand intrinsic wasting (anterior horn cells) + late leg spasticity.

Subacute Combined Degeneration

  • Dorsal columns: Severe sensory ataxia, loss of vibration/proprioception, positive Romberg.
  • Lateral corticospinal: Spastic paraparesis, extensor plantars.
  • Peripheral nerves: Absent ankle jerks (coexisting neuropathy).
Diagnostic Challenge Peripheral Nerve Entrapment Radiculopathy (Spinal Root) Plexopathy / Trunk Lesion
Foot Drop Common Peroneal Nerve: Weak dorsiflexion & eversion. Normal inversion (tibialis posterior) & normal hip abduction. Normal ankle jerk. L5 Radiculopathy: Weak dorsiflexion, eversion, AND weak inversion + weak hip abduction (gluteus medius). Back/radicular pain. Sciatic Nerve / Lumbosacral Plexus: Weak dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion, eversion + weak hamstrings + lost ankle jerk.
Hand Muscle Wasting Ulnar Nerve: Claw hand, interossei weak, spared thenar (APB). Medial 1.5 digit sensory loss.
Median Nerve (CTS): Thenar wasting (APB weak), spared interossei. Palmar digits 1-3.5 sensory loss.		 C8 Radiculopathy: Weakness crosses median + ulnar intrinsics (APB + interossei weak). Medial hand & forearm numbness. Triceps normal. Thoracic Outlet (Lower Trunk): Severe thenar wasting > hypothenar (T1 motor) + medial forearm numbness (C8 sensory). Normal paraspinal EMG.
Shoulder / Arm Weakness Axillary Nerve: Isolated deltoid + teres minor weakness; autonomous patch over lateral shoulder.
Long Thoracic: Winged scapula (serratus anterior).		 C5/C6 Radiculopathy: Weak deltoid, biceps, brachioradialis + reduced biceps reflex + sensory loss to thumb. Erb's Palsy (Upper Trunk C5-C6): "Waiter's tip" arm (adducted, internally rotated, pronated). Biceps + supinator + deltoid lost.

CN III: Pupil-Involving vs Spared

  • Pupil-Involving (Dilated, Fixed): Compressive / surgical lesion (PComm aneurysm, uncal herniation). Parasympathetic fibers run superficially on the nerve periphery.
  • Pupil-Sparing (Reactive): Microvascular ischemia (diabetes, hypertension). Central somatic motor fibers infarcted; peripheral pial blood supply preserves pupillary fibers.

Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO)

  • Unilateral INO: Lesion of ipsilateral MLF. Failure of ipsilateral eye adduction on contralateral horizontal gaze + nystagmus of contralateral abducting eye. Convergence intact!
  • One-and-a-Half Syndrome: Ipsilateral PPRF / CN VI nucleus + ipsilateral MLF. Complete gaze palsy to lesion side + adduction failure to opposite side.
  • WEBINO: Bilateral MLF lesions → bilateral adduction failure with primary position exotropia.

Horizontal Gaze: Cortical vs Pontine

  • Frontal Eye Field (FEF): Eyes look toward the side of the hemispheric lesion (away from hemiparesis). Overcome with oculocephalic reflex (doll's eyes).
  • PPRF / CN VI Nucleus: Eyes look away from the pontine lesion (toward the hemiparesis). Cannot be overcome with doll's eye maneuvers.

Stage 1 — Gross Localisation: Central vs Peripheral (Brain, Cord, or Nerve?)

Learning Objective: Establish fundamental triage: Central (UMN) vs Peripheral (LMN), Brain vs Spinal Cord, Cord vs Roots without eponyms.
Pedagogical Anchor: Finding anchors: Cortical signs -> Cortex; Crossed signs -> Brainstem; Bilateral legs + sensory level -> Cord; Root/nerve LMN -> Peripheral.
12 Cases
6

Proportional Face, Arm, and Leg Weakness Without Cortical Signs

Adult patient • Stage 1: Central vs Peripheral • #1
Clinical Vignette: A 68-year-old man with long-standing hypertension wakes with weakness of the entire right side but has no difficulty speaking or understanding.
Objective Examination Findings:
Right UMN facial weakness
Right arm power 3/5
Right leg power 3/5
Brisk right-sided reflexes
Right extensor plantar response
No aphasia
No neglect
No visual field defect
Normal sensation
✎ Systematic 4-Question Practice Prompts:
Q1. Central or Peripheral? Look for UMN vs LMN signs.
Q2. What Anatomical Level? Cortex, Brainstem, Cord, Roots, Nerve?
Q3. Structures & Tracts? Which pathways lie together here?
Q4. Syndrome / Diagnosis? Correlate spatial locus with pathology.
ⓘ Work through Q1 → Q2 → Q3 → Q4 before revealing the breakdown.
Q1

Question 1: Is the lesion Central or Peripheral?

Central (Deep subcortical / thalamocortical / internal capsule — dense deficits with absent cortical signs).
Clinical clues: Right UMN facial weakness; Right arm power 3/5.
Q2

Question 2: At what Anatomical Level along the neuraxis?

Left internal capsule
Regional cross-section along the cranio-spinal axis.
Q3

Question 3: Which specific structures and tracts are involved?

A dense proportional face-arm-leg weakness without cortical signs strongly suggests compact corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres in the internal capsule.
Anatomical structures that must lie adjacent to produce this combination.
Q4

Question 4: What syndrome / diagnosis best explains this?

pure motor lacunar syndrome
Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.
Teaching Pearl: A dense proportional face-arm-leg weakness without cortical signs strongly suggests compact corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres in the internal capsule.
Anatomical Path & Discriminators: A dense proportional face-arm-leg weakness without cortical signs strongly suggests compact corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres in the internal capsule.
Localisation Anchor: Left internal capsule
Synthesized Localisation
pure motor lacunar syndrome — Left internal capsule

Pure Hemi-Body Sensory Loss Sparing Motor Strength

60-year-old woman suddenly • Stage 1: Central vs Peripheral • #2
Clinical Vignette: A 60-year-old woman suddenly develops numbness affecting the entire left half of her body, including her face.
Objective Examination Findings:
Reduced pinprick and temperature over left face
Similar sensory loss in left arm, trunk and leg
Normal power
Normal reflexes
No aphasia
No neglect

Q1. Central or Peripheral? Look for UMN vs LMN signs.
Q2. What Anatomical Level? Cortex, Brainstem, Cord, Roots, Nerve?
Q3. Structures & Tracts? Which pathways lie together here?
Q4. Syndrome / Diagnosis? Correlate spatial locus with pathology.
ⓘ Work through Q1 → Q2 → Q3 → Q4 before revealing the breakdown.
Q1

Question 1: Is the lesion Central or Peripheral?

Central (Deep subcortical / thalamocortical / internal capsule — dense deficits with absent cortical signs).
Clinical clues: Reduced pinprick and temperature over left face; Similar sensory loss in left arm, trunk and leg.
Q2

Question 2: At what Anatomical Level along the neuraxis?

Right thalamus
Regional cross-section along the cranio-spinal axis.
Q3

Question 3: Which specific structures and tracts are involved?

Face and body sensory loss together without weakness or cortical signs suggests involvement of the thalamic VPM and VPL sensory relay nuclei.
Anatomical structures that must lie adjacent to produce this combination.
Q4

Question 4: What syndrome / diagnosis best explains this?

Right thalamus
Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.
Teaching Pearl: Face and body sensory loss together without weakness or cortical signs suggests involvement of the thalamic VPM and VPL sensory relay nuclei.
Anatomical Path & Discriminators: Face and body sensory loss together without weakness or cortical signs suggests involvement of the thalamic VPM and VPL sensory relay nuclei.
Localisation Anchor: Right thalamus

Dense Leg Weakness with Minimal Arm Involvement and Urinary Incontinence

68-year-old man suddenly • Stage 1: Central vs Peripheral • #3
Clinical Vignette: A 68-year-old man suddenly develops weakness of the left leg. His family also notices that he has become unusually quiet and has urinary urgency.
Objective Examination Findings:
Left leg power 2/5
Left arm power 4+/5
Left lower-limb hyperreflexia
Left extensor plantar response
Grasp reflex present
Reduced spontaneous speech and initiative, without language impairment

Question 4: What syndrome / diagnosis best explains this?

Locked-in syndrome
Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.
Teaching Pearl: Bilateral damage to the ventral pons destroys the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, causing quadriplegia, facial paralysis and anarthria. The dorsal tegmentum — containing the reticular activating system and the pathways for vertical gaze — is spared. Hence the patient remains fully conscious and can communicate only through blinking and vertical eye movements.
Anatomical Path & Discriminators: Bilateral damage to the ventral pons destroys the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, causing quadriplegia, facial paralysis and anarthria. The dorsal tegmentum — containing the reticular activating system and the pathways for vertical gaze — is spared. Hence the patient remains fully conscious and can communicate only through blinking and vertical eye movements.
Localisation Anchor: Bilateral ventral pons (basis pontis)
Synthesized Localisation
Locked-in syndrome — Bilateral ventral pons (basis pontis)

Pedagogical Anchor: Cortical signs (aphasia, apraxia, neglect, visual field defects, agnosias) definitively place lesion in cortex.

Nonfluent Speech with Asymmetric Face and Arm Weakness

Adult patient • Stage 8: Cortex by Lobe • #1
Clinical Vignette: A 70-year-old right-handed man suddenly becomes unable to speak properly and develops weakness of the right face and arm.
Objective Examination Findings:
Speech nonfluent and effortful
Comprehension relatively preserved
Repetition impaired

Right arm power 2/5
Right leg power 4+/5
Right-sided hyperreflexia
✎ Systematic 4-Question Practice Prompts:

Q1

Question 1: Is the lesion Central or Peripheral?

Central (Cerebral cortex — presence of cortical signs such as aphasia, neglect, apraxia, or visual field deficits).
Clinical clues: Speech nonfluent and effortful; Comprehension relatively preserved.
Q2

Question 2: At what Anatomical Level along the neuraxis?

Left frontal lobe
Regional cross-section along the cranio-spinal axis.
Q3

Question 3: Which specific structures and tracts are involved?

Nonfluent aphasia indicates dominant inferior frontal involvement.
Anatomical structures that must lie adjacent to produce this combination.

Question 4: What syndrome / diagnosis best explains this?

dominant hemisphere, Broca region / superior division MCA
Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.
Teaching Pearl: Nonfluent aphasia indicates dominant inferior frontal involvement. Greater face-arm than leg weakness suggests adjacent lateral motor cortex.
Anatomical Path & Discriminators: Nonfluent aphasia indicates dominant inferior frontal involvement. Greater face-arm than leg weakness suggests adjacent lateral motor cortex.
Localisation Anchor: Left frontal lobe
Synthesized Localisation
dominant hemisphere, Broca region / superior division MCA — Left frontal lobe

Oculocephalic reflex restores leftward gaze

Central (Cerebral cortex — presence of cortical signs such as aphasia, neglect, apraxia, or visual field deficits).

Question 2: At what Anatomical Level along the neuraxis?

Right frontal eye field (premotor area 8)
Regional cross-section along the cranio-spinal axis.

Question 3: Which specific structures and tracts are involved?

The frontal eye field drives voluntary conjugate gaze to the opposite side.
Anatomical structures that must lie adjacent to produce this combination.

Question 4: What syndrome / diagnosis best explains this?

Frontal eye field lesion with contralateral hemiparesis
Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.

Anatomical Path & Discriminators: The frontal eye field drives voluntary conjugate gaze to the opposite side. Its destruction causes the eyes to deviate toward the side of the lesion ("the patient looks at their lesion"), while the preserved vestibulo-ocular reflex still moves the eyes contralaterally.

Stage 9 — Deep Hemispheric Lesions: Subcortex, Capsule & Basal Ganglia

Learning Objective: Apply the negative rule: Dense motor/sensory/movement deficits with CONSPICUOUS ABSENCE of cortical signs.
Pedagogical Anchor: Internal capsule -> pure motor; Thalamus -> pure sensory/pain; Subthalamic -> hemiballismus; Substantia nigra -> parkinsonism.

Acute polyradiculoneuropathy — peripheral nerve roots and nerves

Rapidly ascending, symmetric, flaccid weakness with universal areflexia localises to the peripheral nervous system diffusely, not to cord, brain or muscle.

Question 4: What syndrome / diagnosis best explains this?

Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy)
Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.
Teaching Pearl: Rapidly ascending, symmetric, flaccid weakness with universal areflexia localises to the peripheral nervous system diffusely, not to cord, brain or muscle. Antecedent infection (classically Campylobacter), autonomic instability, facial diplegia and later CSF albuminocytological dissociation support the diagnosis.
Anatomical Path & Discriminators: Rapidly ascending, symmetric, flaccid weakness with universal areflexia localises to the peripheral nervous system diffusely, not to cord, brain or muscle. Question 1: Is the lesion Central or Peripheral?

Jugular foramen syndrome — Vernet syndrome
Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.
Teaching Pearl: The glossopharyngeal, vagus and spinal accessory nerves exit the skull together through the jugular foramen. A lesion there — classically a glomus jugulare tumour, fracture or venous thrombosis — produces the combination of: dysphagia with palatal droop and absent gag (IX, X) hoarseness (X) trapezius and sternocleidomastoid weakness (XI) The absence of long-tract signs separates this peripheral skull-base syndrome from a brainstem lesion.

A lesion there — classically a glomus jugulare tumour, fracture or venous thrombosis — produces the combination of: dysphagia with palatal droop and absent gag (IX, X) hoarseness (X) trapezius and sternocleidomastoid weakness (XI) The absence of long-tract signs separates this peripheral skull-base syndrome from a brainstem lesion.

Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.
Teaching Pearl: Combined vagus + hypoglossal palsy without IX or XI involvement points away from the jugular foramen and toward the extracranial course of X and XII. It may follow difficult airway manipulation or prolonged intubation.
Anatomical Path & Discriminators: Combined vagus + hypoglossal palsy without IX or XI involvement points away from the jugular foramen and toward the extracranial course of X and XII. It may follow difficult airway manipulation or prolonged intubation.
Localisation Anchor: Extracranial right CN X and CN XII where they run close together in the upper neck
Synthesized Localisation
Tapia syndrome — Extracranial right CN X and CN XII where they run close together in the upper neck

Question 2: At what Anatomical Level along the neuraxis?

Question 3: Which specific structures and tracts are involved?

A lesion near the facial colliculus can affect: abducens nucleus → ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy looping facial nerve fascicles → ipsilateral LMN facial palsy This combination is highly localising to the dorsal pons.

Ipsilateral Ptosis and Miosis with Contralateral Pain and Temperature Loss

56-year-old man • Stage 10: Master Discriminators • #28
Clinical Vignette: A 56-year-old man develops sudden neck pain followed by unsteadiness and altered sensation on the opposite side of the body.
Objective Examination Findings:
Right-sided partial ptosis
Right pupil smaller than left
Pupillary asymmetry greater in darkness
Facial sweating reduced on right
Reduced pain and temperature over left side of body
Power preserved
No third-nerve palsy
✎ Systematic 4-Question Practice Prompts:
Q1. Central or Peripheral? Look for UMN vs LMN signs.
Q2. What Anatomical Level? Cortex, Brainstem, Cord, Roots, Nerve?

Q1

Question 1: Is the lesion Central or Peripheral?

Central (Brainstem crossed syndrome — ipsilateral cranial nerve nucleus/fascicle + contralateral long tracts).
Clinical clues: Right-sided partial ptosis; Right pupil smaller than left.
Q2

Question 2: At what Anatomical Level along the neuraxis?

Right descending sympathetic pathway in the brainstem
Regional cross-section along the cranio-spinal axis.
Q3

Question 3: Which specific structures and tracts are involved?

Horner syndrome consists of: miosis mild ptosis sometimes anhidrosis When combined with contralateral body sensory abnormalities, it suggests interruption of descending sympathetic fibres within the brainstem, rather than an isolated peripheral sympathetic lesion.
Anatomical structures that must lie adjacent to produce this combination.
Q4

Question 4: What syndrome / diagnosis best explains this?

Central Horner syndrome
Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.
Teaching Pearl: Horner syndrome consists of: miosis mild ptosis sometimes anhidrosis When combined with contralateral body sensory abnormalities, it suggests interruption of descending sympathetic fibres within the brainstem, rather than an isolated peripheral sympathetic lesion.
Anatomical Path & Discriminators: Horner syndrome consists of: miosis mild ptosis sometimes anhidrosis When combined with contralateral body sensory abnormalities, it suggests interruption of descending sympathetic fibres within the brainstem, rather than an isolated peripheral sympathetic lesion.
Localisation Anchor: Right descending sympathetic pathway in the brainstem

Central Horner syndrome — Right descending sympathetic pathway in the brainstem

Weak elbow flexion
Weak wrist extension

Brachioradialis reflex reduced
Sensory loss over lateral forearm and thumb
Triceps strength preserved
Triceps reflex normal

C6 nerve root
Regional cross-section along the cranio-spinal axis.

C6 radiculopathy
Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.
Teaching Pearl: Think C6 when the combination is: biceps/wrist extension weakness + reduced biceps/brachioradialis reflex + thumb sensory symptoms. The distribution crosses more than one peripheral nerve, favouring a root lesion.
Anatomical Path & Discriminators: Think C6 when the combination is: biceps/wrist extension weakness + reduced biceps/brachioradialis reflex + thumb sensory symptoms. The distribution crosses more than one peripheral nerve, favouring a root lesion.

Cape-Like Dissociated Sensory Loss Extending to Facial Analgesia and Bulbar Symptoms

Clinical Vignette: A 42-year-old man with longstanding hand weakness develops progressive numbness of his face, swallowing difficulty and oscillopsia.
Objective Examination Findings:

Pain-temperature loss over outer face in an “onion-skin” distribution
Nystagmus
Palatal weakness
Tongue weakness may occur
Limb vibration relatively preserved

Q2. What Anatomical Level? Cortex, Brainstem, Cord, Roots, Nerve?

Q1

Question 1: Is the lesion Central or Peripheral?

Central (Spinal cord myelopathy — UMN signs below lesion + sensory level ± LMN signs at level).
Clinical clues: Wasting of intrinsic hand muscles; Cape-like pain-temperature loss.
Q2

Question 2: At what Anatomical Level along the neuraxis?

Central cervical cord cavity extending upward into medulla
Regional cross-section along the cranio-spinal axis.
Q3

Question 3: Which specific structures and tracts are involved?

A cervical syrinx extending into the medulla may involve: spinal trigeminal pathways → facial pain-temperature loss vestibular structures → nystagmus lower cranial-nerve nuclei → bulbar weakness The facial findings indicate that a previously spinal process has extended into the brainstem.
Anatomical structures that must lie adjacent to produce this combination.

Syringobulbia accompanying syringomyelia
Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.
Teaching Pearl: A cervical syrinx extending into the medulla may involve: spinal trigeminal pathways → facial pain-temperature loss vestibular structures → nystagmus lower cranial-nerve nuclei → bulbar weakness The facial findings indicate that a previously spinal process has extended into the brainstem.

Clinical Vignette: A 40-year-old man develops severe pain behind the thigh following hip trauma and subsequently develops foot drop.
Objective Examination Findings:
Foot dorsiflexion very weak
Plantarflexion also weak
Inversion and eversion both weak
Hamstring weakness
Knee extension preserved
Ankle jerk absent
Sensory loss over most of foot except medial border
Hip abduction relatively preserved

Q2. What Anatomical Level? Cortex, Brainstem, Cord, Roots, Nerve?

Peripheral (Lower motor neuron / peripheral nerve / plexus / root distribution).

Q2

Question 2: At what Anatomical Level along the neuraxis?

Sciatic nerve
Regional cross-section along the cranio-spinal axis.

Question 3: Which specific structures and tracts are involved?

A common peroneal lesion produces foot drop but preserves plantarflexion.
Anatomical structures that must lie adjacent to produce this combination.

Question 4: What syndrome / diagnosis best explains this?

Sciatic neuropathy
Definitive syndromic classification and clinical entity.
Teaching Pearl: A common peroneal lesion produces foot drop but preserves plantarflexion. An L5 lesion usually preserves the ankle jerk. Combined tibial + peroneal dysfunction with hamstring involvement points proximally to the sciatic nerve.
Anatomical Path & Discriminators: A common peroneal lesion produces foot drop but preserves plantarflexion. An L5 lesion usually preserves the ankle jerk. Combined tibial + peroneal dysfunction with hamstring involvement points proximally to the sciatic nerve.
